summary: This Old House walks through retrofitting HVAC in a 200+ year-old residence with tight spaces and structural constraints. The crew identifies a hidden solution: an oval duct trunk tucked into a pantry to supply a upstairs zone, while ductwork and drains are concealed within walls to preserve historic spaces. They describe sound-attenuation components to quiet the system, a central return strategy, and a plan to finish metals unobtrusively—potentially painting and trimming attenuators to resemble old knot-work. The episode emphasizes a load-driven approach to sizing attenuators and outlets, along with practical tactics for running trunks under joists, hiding drains, and concealing mechanicals behind woodwork for a seamless aesthetic in a historic shell.

sections.title: Initial constraints and trunk location planning
sections.description: The team frames the challenge of adding air conditioning and improved heating in a 200-year-old space, highlighting limited room for hidden ductwork and the need to plan discreetly.

sections.title: Pantry routing and rubble clearing
sections.description: In the original pantry, they describe carving a path for ducts to travel upstairs, including clearing rubble from original joists to allow routing.

sections.title: Trunk routing to upstairs and future bathroom
sections.description: Trunks are traced to the upstairs area and toward a future bathroom, illustrating how ducts are staged within the historic plan.

sections.title: Sound attenuation components
sections.description: Introduction of sound attenuators that provide quiet operation with a cloth-core, including the approach of one attenuator per room and a single central return.

sections.title: Main trunk takeoffs and interlocks
sections.description: They describe making takeoffs from the main trunks, using interlocks, and sealing joints with tape to prevent air loss.

sections.title: Load-based design guideline
sections.description: A rule-of-thumb for sizing: approximately one attenuator/outlet per 10x12 area, tied to the building load.

sections.title: Aesthetic and finish options
sections.description: Discussion of choosing wood types and finishes so the duct hardware can blend with the room’s aesthetics.

sections.title: Aesthetic concealment through trim and finish
sections.description: A proposed method to conceal attenuators by trimming with reclaimed boards and painting the hardware to emulate old knot-work for a quieter, integrated look.
